name: Ladakhi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Francke, A. H. 1901. Sketch of Ladakhi Grammar, in co-operation with other Moravian missionaries. Calcutta: Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 70, Part I, Extra No. 63 pp. (DLI scan, archive.org dli.ministry.06365)
catalog_locator: Introduction, section 'The Accentuation', pp. 6-7; pages read as images
catalog_quote: The Accentuation. Principal rule: When a suffix or the article is joined to a mono-syllabic word, the stem has the stress. Examples: mi'la, to the man; las'la, at work; thsang'ma, all; skam'po, dry; mig'gi, of the eye. Because the words which form a compound throw off their articles before being joined together, most of the compounds consist of only two syllables. In these the first syllable generally has the stress. Examples: chu'mig, well; rkang'lag, limb; lag'shub, glove; nyinlam, day's march; tang'rag, thanks. From the above it follows that the trochee is at the root of all Ladakhi poetic metre. Besides this the dactyl is also rather frequent; for, if a suffix is joined to a compound consisting of two syllables, a dactyl is obtained. There exist a few dissyllabic words in Ladakh which have the stress on the second syllable; for instance: khathog', above; nyerang', you, respectfully; oná, yes (but the latter not in all cases).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (DLI scan, archive.org dli.ministry.06365, 71 pp.) and rendered pp. 14-15 (printed pp. 6-7) as page scan. The section head 'The Accentuation.' closes the Introduction, directly before 'GRAMMAR. THE ARTICLE.' The reported quote is there word for word (ellipses = omitted example words 'nyinlam, day's march; tang'rag, thanks' and the sentence 'Besides this the dactyl is also rather frequent; for, if a suffix is joined to a compound consisting of two syllables, a dactyl is obtained.'): 'Principal rule: When a suffix or the article is joined to a mono-syllabic word, the stem has the stress. Examples: mi'la.. las'la.. thsang'ma.. skam'po.. mig'gi' / 'most of the compounds consist of only t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable: in stem+suffix/article words the monosyllabic stem (initial syllable) is stressed, and in disyllabic compounds the first syllable is generally stressed, giving a trochaic (with a further suffix, dactylic) word rhythm; a handful of disyllabic words are lexically stressed on the second syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress (only that compound + suffix yields a dactyl, i.e. one initial stress over three syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: A few disyllables with second-syllable stress: khathog' 'above', nyerang' 'you (hon.)', oná 'yes' (the last 'not in all cases'). Compounds: first syllable stressed only 'generally'. Separately, Koshal 1976: 14 states stress (with duration, nasalization, tone) is 'non-significant', i.e. non-contrastive, without giving its position.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (stem + suffix/article; two-member compounds); stress marked with an apostrophe after the stressed syllable in cited word forms; linked by the author to poetic metre. Dialect: Leh (per LSI 1909: 'The dialect described in Mr. Francke's grammar.. is that of Leh').
new_statements.identity_note: Francke 1901 describes the Leh dialect (LSI III.1, 1909: 'The dialect described in Mr. Francke's grammar and in the ensuing remarks is that of Leh'), i.e. lada1244 proper, although Francke was stationed at Khalatse (Lower Ladakh/Sham) and occasionally notes Sham/Rong forms. Koshal 1976/1979 describe the Leh (Central) standard. Purik (puri1258; Zemp 2013/2018: verbs sigma-1, nouns sigma-2) and Balti are separate glottocodes and were not used for the statement.
